analysis.one_liner: Mandates offshore oil and gas lease sales and funds highways and water systems with drilling revenue.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote; it was referred to four House committees and its subcommittees in July 2013 and expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Interior Department to open large portions of federal offshore waters to oil and gas leasing, including required sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California. Money from those new leases would partly go to nearby coastal states and would back up to $25 billion a year in federal bonds for highways and water systems. It would also narrow the environmental review required before leasing and reorganize the Interior Department's offshore safety agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain mandated access to unleased federal waters, including at least half the unleased acreage in the most resource-rich offshore planning areas. Coastal states within 200 miles of new leases would receive 37.5 percent of the resulting federal revenue (phased in from 12.5 percent), and Gulf states would get their revenue-sharing payments two years sooner. Highway and water construction would receive a dedicated funding stream through bond proceeds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Offshore oil and gas companies; coastal states; road builders

how_it_helps.text: Dedicates 95 percent of the proceeds of new infrastructure revenue bonds — up to $25 billion per year from 2014 through 2019 — to the Highway Trust Fund, with 2.5 percent each for state wastewater and drinking water programs [S3].
Requires Interior to pay coastal states within 200 miles of new lease tracts a share of new leasing revenue, rising from 12.5 to 37.5 percent, usable by the states for any purpose [S2][S3].
Accelerates Gulf of Mexico energy revenue sharing to Gulf-producing states by two years and raises the annual distribution cap by $250 million [S2][S3].

Reorganizes offshore oversight into a Bureau of Ocean Energy and an Ocean Energy Safety Service, sets inspector qualification and ethics standards, requires random drug testing of affected Interior personnel, and makes offshore operators pay inspection fees to fund the inspection program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury, because leasing revenue from publicly owned waters would be diverted to states and bond repayment instead of the general treasury. Coastal communities and fisheries would bear the spill and disturbance risk from expanded drilling off previously unleased areas, and the bill directs that the required environmental review consider only leasing alternatives, not a no-leasing option. The infrastructure bonds are not backed by the full faith of the United States; if lease revenue falls short, they would not be repaid.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury; coastal communities and fisheries

drawbacks.text: The bill orders a multisale environmental review but expressly removes the requirement to identify or analyze a non-leasing alternative, so the study would not weigh whether to drill at all [S3].
It requires lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California — areas outside the current leasing program — exposing those coastlines to new drilling and its spill risk [S2][S3].

The infrastructure bonds are expressly not guaranteed by the United States and would be paid solely from offshore lease revenue deposited in a dedicated trust account, so road and water funding would depend on drilling revenue materializing as projected [S3].
Sending 37.5 percent of new leasing revenue to coastal states and accelerating Gulf sharing reduces the federal return on resources owned by all Americans [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a genuine public need — dedicated road and water funding — with expanded drilling on public waters, and the design ties the public benefit to the industry benefit: the roads get paid only if companies drill. It also short-circuits environmental review by barring consideration of a no-leasing alternative, and it shifts a large share of the resource revenue away from the treasury. Someone who wants more domestic drilling and infrastructure spending would see this as a reasonable package; the honest objection is that it commits coastal areas to drilling risk before the question of whether to drill there was ever fully weighed.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees and divided among their subcommittees, the bill was never brought up for a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stivers introduced the bill on July 22, 2013, joined by Rep. Cedric Richmond [S1][S3].
The same day, the House referred it to four committees — Natural Resources, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce [S5].
Within days it was sent to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment, Highways and Transit, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Environment and the Economy [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; the record shows no action after the subcommittee referrals [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new lease sales were mandated off Virginia, South Carolina, or Southern California, federal offshore revenue was not redirected to states and bond repayment, and the environmental review process was not narrowed. The oil and gas industry did not gain the access it sought; coastal areas were spared the new drilling risk, but the proposed infrastructure funding also never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal areas stayed unleased; no drilling-driven bonds

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor from a Gulf drilling state, but since no committee or floor vote ever occurred, the record shows no party-split vote on it.

industries.note: The bill would lock offshore drilling in as the dedicated funding channel for federal highway and water spending, while mandating lease sales covering at least half the unleased acreage in the richest planning areas plus specific sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California. It narrows environmental review by barring a no-leasing alternative, though it also imposes new inspection fees and safety oversight on operators [S2][S3].
Ninety-five percent of up to $25 billion per year in bond proceeds would flow to the Highway Trust Fund, creating a dedicated stream for road and transit work [S3].

industries.industry: Water and wastewater construction and utilities
industries.note: Five percent of bond proceeds would fund state revolving loan funds for wastewater treatment and drinking water systems [S3].

Mandated lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California would introduce drilling near coastlines whose beaches and fisheries depend on clean water, with the required environmental study barred from weighing a no-drilling option [S2][S3].
